paragraphs.text: Five Orations on Holy Easter and on the Three-Day Interval of the Resurrection of Christ

If there is any blessing of the patriarchs that draws its certainty from the divine Spirit; if any good of the spiritual law is hoped for, by promise, by those who live rightly; if any foreshadowing of the truth is believed to lie in the riddles of the historical narratives; if any prophetic voice proclaims the good news of things beyond nature, all of these belong to the present grace. And just as, in the

spectacle set before our eyes, a single light shines all around, gathering its brightness from countless lamps, so the whole blessing of Christ, each part shining by itself like a torch, produces for us this great light, blended from the many and varied rays of Scripture. For from each of the divinely inspired proofs one can take what suits the present holy festival. Are you looking for the blessing of Abraham? You have what you are looking for when you look at what is before you. "Do you see the stars of heaven?" I mean these stars, which have just now risen from our Father and have all at once made the Church a heaven, and whose flashing grace of soul is shown by the rays of their torches. Anyone who says that these are truly the children of Abraham, born to him by promise and likened to the stars of heaven, will not miss the truth. And do you admire the lofty Moses, who took in the whole creation of God by the power of his knowledge? Here you have the blessed Sabbath of the world's first creation. Through that Sabbath recognize this Sabbath, the day of rest, which God blessed above the other days. For on this day the Only-begotten God truly rested from all his works. He kept Sabbath in the flesh through the dispensation of death, and then, returning again to what he was, through the resurrection he raised up with himself all that lay fallen, and became life and resurrection and dawn and day to those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death. The story of the kindred blessing is full indeed: the father who does not spare that beloved Isaac, the only son who becomes an offering and a sacrifice, and the lamb slaughtered in his place. For in this story one can see the whole mystery of godliness. The lamb hangs from the wood, caught by its horns, while the only son carries on himself the wood for the whole burnt offering. You see: he who bears all things by the word of his power is the same who carries the load of our wood, and is lifted up by the wood. He carries as God, and is carried as the lamb. Thus the Holy Spirit divided the great mystery in figure between the two, the beloved Son and the sheep shown alongside him, so that the mystery of death was shown in the sheep, and in the only son the life that death does not cut short. And if you wish to take Moses himself, tracing the cross by stretching out his hands, with Amalek overthrown as it were by this figure, you can see the type in the reality, and Amalek falling beneath the cross. You also have Isaiah, who contributes no small part to the present grace. For from him you were taught beforehand about the unwedded mother, the fatherless flesh, the painless labor, the undefiled birth. For thus the Prophet says: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name

Emmanuel, which means, God with us." That the birth took place without pain, let reason teach you first. Since every pleasure has pain joined to it, it follows necessarily, in all things that are seen as joined together, that where one is absent, the other is absent too. Where, then, pleasure did not go before the birth, pain did not follow it either. Then the Prophet's own words also confirm the point, for they run thus: "Before the pain of her labor came, she escaped it and bore a male child." Or, as another of the translators puts it, "Before she was in labor, she gave birth." From this virgin mother, he says, "a child was born to us, and a son was given to us, whose government was upon his shoulder, the Angel of great counsel," and so on. This child, this son, "was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer"; or rather, as Jeremiah says, this is the innocent lamb led to be sacrificed. This is the bread into which they cast the wood, they who are enemies both of the bread and of the wood. But let us rather take what is most familiar and evident of all from the Prophet through whom the mystery is clearly prefigured: Jonah, I mean, who went down into the sea monster without suffering and came up out of the monster unharmed, and who, by spending three days and as many nights in the monster's belly, prefigured the Lord's sojourn in Hades. These and similar things you must search out and gather from every Scripture. For all of them you see in what is before you, and on this present radiant feast "hang the whole law and the prophets," as the Gospel says somewhere; and every divinely inspired word and law is summed up in this grace, as Paul says. For this is both the end of sorrows and the beginning of good things. I mean something like this: "Death reigned from Adam," who gave its corrupting power its start, and its wicked rule lasted even until Moses, for the law did nothing to blunt death's evil dominion. Then the kingdom of life came, and the power of death was destroyed. And there came about another birth, a different life, another kind of living, a transformation of our very nature. This birth is "not of blood, nor of the will of a man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God." How so? I will set this grace clearly before you in words. This child is conceived through faith; it is brought into the light through the rebirth of baptism; its nurse is the Church; its breast, her teachings; its food, the bread from above; its coming of age, the lofty way of life; its marriage, life shared with wisdom; its children, its hopes; its house, the kingdom; its inheritance and wealth, the delight of paradise; and its end, in place of death, eternal life in the blessedness laid up for the saints. The great Zechariah too sees this beginning of the change toward the good, and is at a loss what name to give it, what properly to call the

present grace. For after going through the other wonders surrounding the passion, he says this too about this season: "It is not day, and it is not night." By this he shows that it cannot be called day, since there is no sun, and that it is not night, since there is no darkness either. For God called the darkness night, as Scripture says

Since, then, by the hour it is night, but by the light it is day, the Prophet says for this reason: "And it is not day, and it is not night." If, then, according to the Prophet's word, this season is neither night nor day, the present grace must surely be, and be named, something other than these. Would you like me to tell you what I have been pondering? "This is the day which the Lord has made"; it is a different day from those at the beginning. For on this day God makes a new heaven and a new earth, as the Prophet says. What heaven? The firmament of faith in Christ. What earth? I mean the good heart, as the Lord said, the earth that drinks the rain falling upon it and ripens the rich ear of grain. In this creation the sun is the pure life; the stars, the virtues; the air, the transparent way of life; the sea, the depth of the riches of wisdom and knowledge; the grass and green shoots, good teaching and the divine doctrines, on which the people of his pasture, that is, the flock of God, feed; and the fruit-bearing trees, the doing of the commandments. In this creation the true man is made, the one who comes into being after the image and likeness of God. Is not this beginning a world for you, "the day which the Lord has made"? Of it the prophet Zechariah says that it is neither a day like the other days nor a night like the other nights. And the discourse has not yet proclaimed what is most remarkable about the present grace. This day loosed the pangs of death. This day brought to birth the firstborn of the dead. On this day the iron gates of death were shattered. On this day the bronze bars of Hades were broken. Now the prison of death is opened. Now release is proclaimed to the captives. Now sight is restored to the blind. Now the dawn from on high visits those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death. Would you like to learn something about the three-day interval as well? It is enough to learn this much: that in so short a span of time the all-powerful Wisdom, the Lord, having come into the heart of the earth, was enough to make a fool of that great mind which dwelt there. For that is the name the Prophet gives him, calling him "the great mind" and "the Assyrian." Since, then, the heart is a kind of hearth of the mind (for the ruling faculty is believed to reside in it), the Lord for this reason comes into the heart of the earth, which is the [?] dwelling-place of that mind, so as to make his counsel foolish, as the Prophet says, to catch the wise in his own craftiness, and to turn his clever schemes back against him. For since it was impossible for the ruler of darkness

to come into contact with the unmixed presence of the light unless he saw some portion of flesh in it, when he saw the God-bearing flesh, and saw also the wonders of the divinity worked through it, he hoped that if he could overpower the flesh through death, he would also overpower all the power within it. And for this reason, gaping at the bait of the flesh, he was pierced by the hook of the divinity, and so the dragon was drawn out by the hook, as Job says, who foretold through his own person what was to come, saying, "You will draw out the dragon with a hook." Let us hear from the voice of the Prophet what this heart of the earth plotted against the universe when it opened its mouth against the flesh of the Lord. What does Isaiah say to him in reproof? "You said in your heart: I will ascend into heaven, I will set my throne above the clouds, and I will be like the Most High." These are the things the wicked heart plotted against itself. And let us hear again from the voice of Isaiah what, even before this, the mind great in wickedness, the wicked Assyrian, rehearsed to himself. This is what he said: "By the strength of my hand I will do it, and by the wisdom of my understanding I will remove the boundaries of nations and plunder their strength; I will shake inhabited cities, and seize the whole world like a nest, and carry it off like abandoned eggs, and there is no one who will escape me or speak against me." With this hope he receives into himself the one who, out of love for humankind, had come to dwell among those below. What he got instead of what he had hoped for, the prophecy tells clearly when it describes what befell him: "How has the morning star fallen from heaven? How has he been crushed to the earth, he under whom rottenness is spread, whose garment is a covering of worms?" and everything else it relates about his destruction, which anyone who wishes can learn in detail from the Scriptures themselves. But I must bring my discourse back to its purpose. This is why the true Wisdom comes into this boastful heart of the earth: to wipe out from it the mind great in wickedness, so that the darkness might be lit up, the mortal swallowed up by life, and evil pass away into nothingness, once the last enemy, which is death, has been destroyed. This is what the three-day interval has accomplished for you. Is the grace slow? Has so great a good been achieved only over a very long period? Do you want to know how surpassing is the power shown in what was accomplished in so short a time? Count for me all the generations of humankind in between, from the first entrance of evils until their undoing, how many people there were in each generation, numbered in how many tens of thousands. It is impossible to grasp by number the multitude through whose successions wickedness spread ever wider. The evil wealth of wickedness, divided out to each person, grew greater through each one, and so, multiplying

itself, wickedness moved on with each succeeding generation, poured out in ever greater quantity without limit, until, having advanced to the very height of evil, it took hold of all human nature. So the Prophet declared universally: "All have turned aside, together they have become worthless," and there was nothing among all that exists that was not an instrument of wickedness. Then he who in three days scattered so great a heap of evil, piled up from the foundation of the world until the dispensation of the Lord's passion: has he given you a small display of surpassing power? Is it not mightier than all the wonder-workers in the histories? For just as Samson's wonder is the greater, not only because he overpowered the lion, but because he dispatched it without effort, tearing the beast apart with bare, unarmed hands as if in play, so too the Lord's wiping out of so much wickedness without any toil at all is the greater proof of his surpassing power. It was not floods of boundless waters pouring down from the floodgates above onto what lay below, nor the deeps swelling beyond their own bounds and drowning the land under seas, nor the whole inhabited world covered by the abyss like a ship lost with all hands, nor mountains sinking to the sea floor and mountaintops under water; nor, as at Sodom, showers of flame purging the corruption with fire; nor anything else of that kind. Rather, a single, simple, and incomprehensible coming, the presence of life and light to those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, alone brought about the total eclipse and destruction of both darkness and death. Shall I add something else to what has been said? Evil sprang up in the serpent; the woman was overcome by the dragon's temptation; afterward the man was overcome by the woman. Evil came into being through three. What does recalling this point to? One can discern a certain order of the good through the order found in evil. I see these three as the vessels of evil: first, the one in which it first arose; second, the one into which it flowed over; third, the one in which it came about after that. Since, then, wickedness flooded these three, I mean the devil's nature, the race of women, and the whole company of men, it follows fittingly that the disease is wiped out in three days, one day being allotted for healing to each kind of those sick with wickedness. On one day men are cleansed of the disease; on the second the race of women is healed; on the last, the last enemy, death, is destroyed, and together with him the rulers and authorities and powers of the hostile forces and of those who preside over them are wiped out. Do not be surprised if the creation of the good is spread over intervals of time. For at the first creation of the world, too, the divine power was not too weak to bring all things to completion in an instant, yet it nonetheless took up intervals of time in making all things, so that one part of creation was completed on the first day

and another on the second, and likewise all things were brought to completion in order, God fitting together the whole creation in set days. So here too, by the ineffable reason of his wisdom, evil is evicted from what exists in three days: from men, from women, and from the race of serpents, in which the nature of wickedness first had its origin. Concerning the reason for the number of days, then, this is what we have conjectured; whether rightly or not, we leave to the judgment of our hearers. For this discourse is not a final ruling, but an exercise and an inquiry. But if you want to see precisely the interval of these days in the passion (for the count falls quite a bit short if you reckon the time from the ninth hour of the Day of Preparation, when he committed his spirit into his Father's hands), wait a little, and perhaps the discourse will make this clear to you. What, then, is the explanation? Look up to the majesty of the divine power, and you will not be ignorant of what is being sought here. Remember the Master's declaration, what he on whom the might of the universe depends declares about himself: how by sovereign authority, and not by necessity of nature, he separates the soul from the body, when he says, "No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again." Let this stand firm for me, and what we are seeking becomes clear. For he who orders all things by his sovereign authority does not wait for the compulsion of the betrayal, the bandit-like assault of the Jews, and Pilate's lawless judgment, as though their wickedness were to become the origin and cause of the common salvation of humankind. Rather, by his dispensation he anticipates their assault, in the ineffable manner of the sacred rite, invisible to human eyes, and offered himself as an offering and sacrifice for us, being at once the priest and the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. When did this happen? When he showed his own body to be edible as food, he clearly demonstrated that the sacrifice of the lamb had already been completed. For the body of a sacrificial victim would not be fit to eat if it were still alive. So when he gave his disciples his body to eat and his blood to drink, already, in accordance with the will and authority of him who was administering the mystery, his body had been sacrificed, ineffably and invisibly. And his soul was in the place where the authority of the one administering it had laid it, together with the divine power mingled with it, ranging through that region in the heart of the earth. So anyone who counts the time from the moment the sacrifice was offered to God by the great High Priest, who ineffably and invisibly sacrificed his own lamb for the sin of all, will not miss the truth. For it was evening when that sacred and holy body was eaten. That evening was followed by the night before the Day of Preparation. Then the Day of Preparation, cut through by the inserted

night, is reckoned as one night and two days. For if God called the darkness night, and for three hours there was darkness over the whole world, this is the night newly introduced in the middle of the day, which marks off two segments of daytime, one from dawn to the sixth hour, the other from the ninth hour to evening. So up to this point there are two nights and two days. Then comes the night before the Sabbath, and after it the day of the Sabbath: there you have the three nights. Now look for me for the hour of the resurrection, and you will find the truth of what has been said. When, then, was it? "Late on the Sabbath," Matthew cries. This indeed is the hour of the Resurrection, according to the voice of the angel. This is the limit of the Lord's stay in the heart of the earth. For when evening had already deepened (and the evening was the beginning of that night which the first day of the week follows), then the earthquake happens. Then the angel, flashing like lightning in his garments, rolls the stone away from the tomb. And the women, rising a little early, when the light of day was already appearing, so that some gleam of the sun was showing above the east, then learn of the resurrection that had already taken place. They knew of the wonder, but were not told the hour. For the angel told them that he had risen, but did not add in his words when. But the great Matthew alone of all the evangelists marked the time precisely, saying that the hour of the Resurrection was the evening of the Sabbath. If this is how things stand, our interval holds firm: the time is measured from the evening after the fifth day to the evening of the Sabbath, with the inserted night, as has been said, cutting the Day of Preparation into two days and one night. For it was fitting that, in the case of him who rules over the age by his sovereign power, his works should not be forced to stretch out along the fixed measures of time; rather, the measures of time should be made new to meet the needs of things, and, since the divine power accomplished its good work more swiftly, the measures of time should be laid out in shorter form. Thus the time is not counted as less than three days and as many nights, since the mystical and secret reason requires this number, and yet the divine power is not hindered in the swiftness of its working by having to wait for the usual spans of days and nights. For he who had authority both to lay down his soul of himself and to take it up again when he wished, had authority, as the maker of the ages, not to be a slave to time in his works, but to make time according to his works. But the discourse has not yet touched on the greatest of its main points. For the more studious will naturally ask how, at the same time, the Lord gives himself to three: to the heart of the earth and to the

in paradise with the thief, and in the Father's hands. For to the Pharisees he says, "As Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth," for the space of three days. To the thief he says, "Today you will be with me in paradise." And to the Father he says, "Into your hands I commit my spirit." No one would place paradise in the regions under the earth, or the regions under the earth in paradise, so that he could be in both at once, or call these places the Father's hand. Among those who reason piously, perhaps this does not even deserve inquiry. For he who is everywhere through his divine power is present to everything and absent from nothing. But I have learned another explanation of this as well, and if you wish I will set it out for you briefly. When [?] the Holy Spirit [came upon?] the Virgin and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, so that the new man might be formed in her (he is called new because he was created according to God and not according to human custom, so as to become a vessel for God not made with hands; for the Most High does not dwell in things made with hands, meaning things built by men), then, as Wisdom was building her house for them [?], and it was shaped within by the overshadowing of the power as if by the impress of a seal, the divine power was blended with both of the things that make up human nature, namely soul and body, mingling itself fittingly with each. Both of these had been put to death through disobedience, since the death of the soul was its estrangement from true life, and the death of the body was corruption and dissolution. So it was necessary for death to be driven out of both by the mingling of life with them. And since the Godhead was mingled fittingly with each of the two parts of the human being, the marks of the higher nature were evident through both. The body showed the Godhead within it by effecting cures through touch, and the soul displayed the divine power through that mighty will. For as the sense of touch belongs properly to the body, so movement by choice belongs properly to the soul. The leper comes to him, his body already wasting away and made useless. How does the Lord accomplish the healing in this case? The soul wills, and the body . . . [?] the leprosy. Again, he does not want to send away fasting the many thousands who had waited on him in the wilderness, and he breaks the loaves with his hands. Do you see how the Godhead that accompanied each part is made known through both, through the body acting and through the impulse of the will arising in the soul? But why go through all the miracles performed in the same way and occupy the discourse with what is obvious? I will move on to the point for whose sake I recalled these things. How is the Lord in Hades and in paradise at the same time? One solution to this question is that nothing is inaccessible to God, in whom all things hold together. Another

is the one the discourse now has in view. God had transformed the whole human being into the divine nature by blending it with himself. At the time of the dispensation of the Passion, what had once been blended did not withdraw from either part, for the gifts of God are irrevocable. The Godhead willingly separated the soul from the body, but showed that it remained in both. Through the body, in which he did not undergo the corruption of death, he destroyed the one who had the power of death. Through the soul he opened the way for the thief to enter paradise. The two things are accomplished at the same time, with the Godhead achieving the good through both. Through the incorruptibility of the body comes the destruction of death, and through the soul hastening to its own home comes humanity's return to paradise. The human compound is twofold, while the nature of the Godhead is simple and uniform. So when the body is separated from the soul, the indivisible is not split along with the composite. The reverse happens: through the unity of the divine nature, which is present equally in both, the separated parts grow together again. In this way death comes from the division of what had grown together, and resurrection from the union of what had been divided. If you ask how, while he is in paradise, he commits himself into the Father's hands, the sublime Isaiah will explain the question for you. Speaking in the person of God about the Jerusalem above, which we believe is none other than paradise, he said: "On my hands I have painted your walls." If, then, Jerusalem, which is paradise, is drawn on the Father's hands, then clearly he who came to be in paradise certainly dwells in the Father's palms, where the divine city has its outline. And so much for

It would be worth adding something briefly to the discourse about the charges we hear from the Jews as they vehemently attack our teaching. They say that in the law of the Passover Moses prescribed for the Jews the fourteenth day of the lunar cycle, the eating of unleavened bread for seven days, and the use of bitter herbs as a relish with the unleavened bread. "If, then," says the Jew, "you are careful to observe the fourteenth day, observe the bitter herb and the unleavened bread along with it. But if these deserve to be disregarded, why are you so zealous about the other? Surely the same lawgiver's commands cannot be judged partly just and profitable for the soul, and partly useless and fit to be thrown away. So either we must fulfil everything prescribed concerning the Passover, or we must hold to none of it." What, then, do we say? Let us remember the one who commanded us not to fear the reproach of men or be overcome by their contempt. For we know that the observance of unleavened bread profits the soul, and we know the benefit of the bitter herbs

and the usefulness of the fourteenth day. This is the reasoning, which we will examine briefly. The law, which has the shadow of the good things to come, looks above all to one aim: that through its various commandments the human being might be cleansed of the evil mixed into him. This aim is achieved in circumcision, in the Sabbath, in the observance concerning foods, in the various animal sacrifices, and in each of the law's particular observances. It would take a long time for us to set out in detail what the law indicates in riddles about each of these for the purification of life. Through circumcision performed spiritually, nature lays aside passion and strips off the fleshly life. Through keeping the Sabbath it learns to be inactive in evil. The animal sacrifice slaughters the passions, and the prescribed distinction concerning [?] unclean animals counsels you to keep away from a filthy and unclean life. In the same way this feast points you to that other feast, for which the soul prepares itself through the unleavened bread by keeping clear of leavened food for seven days. Their riddle is this. The number of seven days shows you this passing time, which comes round again in weeks. In it we must take care that no remnant of yesterday's evil is carried over into the present day, so that stale evil does not cause sourness and acidity in today's dough. "Do not let the sun go down on your anger," says the Apostle, who bids us keep the feast not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. What we have learned about this one kind of evil we are taught to apply by analogy to the other kinds. The bitter herb drives out what is slack and dissolute in life and brings in its place a life that is self-controlled, hardened and unpleasant to the senses. For no discipline seems joyful at the time, but grievous. Throughout the whole week of this life, he keeps each present day unmixed with old evil and unleavened, and makes self-control the relish of his life. Such a person separates himself from all admixture of darkness. This is what the fourteenth day of the lunar course shows. The days of the lunar course number twenty-nine and a half in all. During them the moon grows from the new moon until its orb is complete, and then wanes again until its light is entirely gone. Half of that number, then, is fourteen and a little more. So when the moon is in this phase, it advances along its own course during the night and adds what its orb was lacking. Filled with light, it mingles its own brightness with the rays of the day, so that neither in the evening

nor at dawn does any intrusion of darkness break the continuity of light; the brightness remains undivided as one luminary succeeds the other. Before the sun's ray has quite set, the moon appears directly opposite the sun across the diameter and lights what lies below with its own light. And again, before its orb has gone entirely below the horizon, the brightness of day mingles with the remnants of the moonlight. So on that day of the full moon darkness vanishes at both dawn and evening, made bright by the succession of the luminaries. On the fourteenth day the visible light admits no admixture of darkness through the whole night and day. The spiritual law wants this to become a symbol for those who keep the feast spiritually. Throughout the week of life they are to make the whole time of their life a single Passover, full of light and without darkness. This is what the precepts concerning the Passover establish for Christians. That is why we look to the fourteenth day. From this sensible, material light we take an image of the immaterial and intelligible light. We seem to be seeking a full moon that gives us steady light all night long. In truth, the observance is a law for us that all our time, measured out in night and day, should be continually bright and unmixed with the works of darkness. So much for these matters. But who could easily put into words all the meanings contained in the cross, through which the mystery of the Passion is completed? Were there not countless ways leading to death by which the dispensation of death on our behalf could have been fulfilled? Yet out of them all, this one was appointed by the very one who, by his own authority, appointed his Passion for himself. For he says, "The Son of Man must." He did not say, "The Son of Man will suffer such and such things," as someone might say when simply foretelling an event. By this word he lays down as doctrine that it was necessary and had to happen for some ineffable reason, when he says, "The Son of Man must suffer many things, be rejected, be crucified, and rise on the third day." Consider with me the meaning of "must." Through it we find that the Passion so declared had to take place through the cross and in no other way. What, then, is the reason for this? Only the great Paul can make the mystery of this plain. He was taught the unspeakable words he heard when he was initiated in the inner sanctuaries of paradise, and he partly hinted at the hidden meaning in his letter to the Ephesians, saying: "That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and depth and height, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled with all the fullness of God." For it was not idly that the Apostle's divine eye

contemplated the shape of the cross. Through this he showed clearly that whoever has cast the scales of ignorance from his eyes sees truth itself with pure sight. He knows that this figure is divided into four arms from the junction in the middle. It signifies the power and providence of the one who appeared upon it, which reaches through all things. For this reason he gives each arm its own name. He calls the part running down from the middle "depth" and the part above "height." He calls "breadth" and "length" what extends sideways on either side of the junction, so that the part on one side of the middle is breadth and the part on the other is length. By these words he seems to me to signify clearly that nothing exists that is not held together by the divine nature: what lies above the heavens, what lies under the earth, and what stretches sideways in every direction to the ends of all that exists. By "height" he signifies what lies above, by "depth" what is under the earth, and by length and breadth the limits in between, which are held together by the power that holds all things. Let what happens in your own soul when you think about God prove what has been said. Look up to heaven, and consider in thought the depths below. Stretch your mind to the sides and the extremities of the whole frame of the universe, and reckon what power holds all these together and becomes, as it were, the bond of the universe. You will see that the concept of the divine power traces the shape of the cross in your mind of its own accord, reaching down from the heights to the depths and stretching crosswise to the farthest ends. The great David too praised this figure in his own words: "Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend to heaven" (this is the height); "if I descend to Hades" (this is the depth); "if I take my wings at dawn," that is, at the rising of the sun (this is the breadth); "if I dwell in the farthest parts of the sea" (this is how he names the west; this is the length). Do you see how he paints the shape of the cross in these words? "You," he says, "are the one who reaches through all things. You are the bond of all that comes to be, and you hold all the extremities within yourself. You are above, you are present below, your hand is at this end, and at the other your right hand guides." For this reason the great Apostle, where everything belonging to faith and knowledge is fulfilled [?], says that he who is above every name is worshipped in the name of Jesus Christ by things in heaven, things on earth and things under the earth. Here again he divides the worship of the cross according to the shape of the cross. The order above the world offers worship to the Master in the upper part of the cross, the order within the world in the middle, and the order under the earth keeps to the depth. In my view, this is also the iota

seen together with its stroke, which is more lasting than the heavens, firmer than the earth, and more enduring than the whole frame of existing things. "Heaven and earth will pass away," and "the form of this whole world is passing away"; but the iota and the stroke of the law do not pass away. The vertical line, which runs down from above to the depth, is called the iota. The line drawn crosswise from the side is called the stroke (keraia), as one can learn from sailors. They call the beam lying crosswise on the mast, on which they spread the sail, the keraia, the yard, naming it from its shape. So it seems to me that the divine voice of the Gospel has this in view. That in which all things hold together is more everlasting than the things it holds within it. Through the shape of the cross, as in a riddle and a mirror, it shows its own power that preserves all existing things. This is why he says that the Son of Man must not simply die but be crucified. For those with keener sight, the cross thus becomes a theologian, proclaiming by its shape the almighty authority of the one who was displayed upon it and who is all in all. Let us not pass over in silence, brothers, that honourable councillor, Joseph of Arimathea. He received that undefiled and holy body as a gift, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth, and laid it in a clean tomb. Let the deed of that honourable councillor be a law for us, so that we too take similar counsel. When we receive that gift of the body, we must not receive it in the soiled linen of our conscience, or lay it in the tomb of a heart that stinks of dead bones and all uncleanness. Rather, as the Apostle says, let each one examine himself, so that the grace does not become judgment for one who receives it unworthily. But even as I speak I feel the radiant robe of the angel flashing upon me, and that sweet earthquake shakes my heart with joy. It rolls away the heavy stone of the human tomb, and through it the door of resurrection is opened to all. Let us too run to see this wondrous sight. The Sabbath is already past; let us not arrive after the women. We too will have spices in our hands, faith and conscience, for these are the fragrance of Christ. Let us no longer seek the living among the dead. The Lord pushes away the one who seeks him in this way [?], saying: "Do not touch me; but when I ascend to the Father, then you may touch me." Let us hear the good news that the woman proclaims as well. She went ahead of the man through faith, and she was right to do so, so that by taking the lead toward the good she might make amends for having been the cause of evil. What, then, is the woman's gospel? Truly it is not from men or through men, but through Jesus Christ. "Hear," she says, "what the Lord has commanded us to tell you" (you whom he even calls his brothers): "I am going to my

Father and your Father, to my God and your God." O fair and good tidings! For our sake he became like us, so that by becoming of our kind he might make us his brothers. He brings his own humanity to the true Father, so that through it he may draw along everyone of his kind. Then those who served beings that are not gods by nature need no longer bear reproach. Because they have been brought back to the living and true God, those who have followed the Son through adoption are no longer rejected and disinherited from their Father's inheritance. He who through the flesh made himself the firstborn among many brothers drew to himself all creation, in which he shared through the flesh blended with him. But since the unleavened bread before the Passover has the bitter herb as its relish, let us see what seasoning sweetens the bread after the resurrection. Do you see [?] . . . To solve the problem before us, and the other questions that arise when the texts are examined, we must be roused by the risen God, weak though we are, to present a clear interpretation. He who has sown the seed of the reading and spread it in everyone's hearing is rightly obliged to account for the questions that have sprung up from it. This I will try to do, drawing the solution from the very statements of those who raised the difficulty. The holy writers of the Gospels did not say that the Lord rose late on the Sabbath, or when most of the night had passed, or at dawn, or after the sun's ray had shone forth. If they had, there would be a contradiction, since the writers would not be describing the one event with one [?]

[?] …but as having reported that these things happened at different times. Rather, they wrote that the women came to the tomb at different times and in different ways, not at one and the same time. For how could women who came at different times all alike have heard from the angels about the Saviour, "He has risen, he is not here," without any statement of when? The resurrection, as all admit and agree, took place on that divine night. But no one marked the hour. It is unknown to all except the God who rose, and the Father, who alone knows the Son in this way, as he himself is known to the [?], and the Spirit, who searches all things, even the depths of God. Matthew said that Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came late on the Sabbath to see the tomb, and that there was a great earthquake. An angel came down from heaven, his appearance like lightning and his clothing like snow. The fearsome part was to terrify the guards, who could not bear the sight and nearly perished, becoming like dead men from fear. The radiant part was to call the women to him, to give courage to those who are by nature easily frightened and timid, and by his very appearance to announce the resurrection with joy. For it was for these purposes too that he had been sent. When he rolled away the stone he found the Lord already risen. In a manner befitting God, the Lord had left the tomb while it was still closed, secured with seals and guarded by the soldiers' watch, just as he came to the disciples when he entered the room while the doors were shut. That is why the angel said, "He is not here, but has risen." He was indicating that the Saviour's resurrection had been miraculously accomplished before he himself arrived. The Saviour accomplished it by his own power as God, carrying out the dispensation without needing help from angels. If this were not so, the angel would have said, "Behold, he is rising," showing something happening at that moment. But since it had already happened, he used the past tense and said, "He is not here, but has risen." From this it is also clearly shown that when the apostles preached the gospel and said that Christ had been raised by the Father, they did so because of the weakness of their hearers, making the message easy to receive in this way. But the angel, breaking into the voice that announced the good news of the resurrection, displayed openly the most godlike authority of the one who rose, and cried out, "He is not here, but has risen." To say that he was raised by the Father makes allowance, as I said, for the weakness of the hearers, but it has the same meaning and no other. For by what does the Father act? By his own power, clearly. And what is the power of the Father? None other than Christ, for Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Therefore the Saviour raised himself, even if he is said to have been raised by the Father. Now "late on the Sabbath" does not mean the evening at sunset, for he did not say, in the singular,

"late on the Sabbath," but in the plural, "late on the Sabbaths." The Hebrews customarily call the whole week "Sabbaths." For example, the evangelists say "on the first of the Sabbaths," meaning "on the first day of the week." We use the same expression in our ordinary speech, calling the second and third days of the week "the second of the Sabbaths" and "the third of the Sabbaths." So he did not say "late on the Sabbath" or "on the evening of the Sabbath," which would mean the evening of that day, but "late on the Sabbaths," to show lateness and a long lapse of time. Indeed we commonly say, "You have come late in the season," "late in the hour," "late for what was needed." These expressions do not mean the evening and the time after sunset. They mean that something happened late, after the need or the right moment had passed. So "late on the Sabbaths" means the far and late end of the completed week. Each week is completed at sunset after the Sabbath. Matthew shows how far the time had advanced toward the end of the completed week, and, as if interpreting himself, he added, "as it was dawning toward the first of the Sabbaths." The night, he means, had advanced so far that it was the time of cockcrow, which heralds the light of the coming day. This is why we break the fasts and begin the festival at this hour and not on the evening after the Sabbath, and the custom that has prevailed everywhere supports this. At this hour, then, Mary Magdalene and her namesake came to the tomb. They saw the angel who had come down from heaven in the manner already described, who had rolled away the stone and was sitting on it. When he called them forward, they saw the place where the Lord had lain. When he told them to run and tell the disciples, they went out quickly from the tomb and ran. As they ran, Jesus met them and greeted them: "Rejoice!" For it was fitting that womankind should be the first to have the resurrection announced to them by the angel, to see the Lord, and to hear his first word, "Rejoice!" For a woman was also the first to hear the serpent's deceit, and lawlessly looked on the fruit of the forbidden tree, and was condemned to sorrow. That is why the Saviour allowed them to worship him and hold his feet, since they had been the first to fall away and be estranged from him. He told them to announce the joy to the disciples, wishing a woman, who had become the minister of sorrow to Adam, to become the messenger of joy to men, healing opposites by opposites. "As they were going to tell the disciples," he says, "behold, some of the guard came

into the city and told the chief priests all that had happened. When they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave a large sum of money to the soldiers and said, 'Say that his disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep. And if this comes to the governor's ears, we will persuade him and keep you out of trouble.' So they took the money and did as they were told, and this story has been spread among the Jews to this day." Now the other Mary fulfilled the Lord's command and certainly reported to the disciples. It is reasonable to believe that this was the Theotokos. She was not absent from the passion either, but stood by the cross, as John records. It was fitting that she should announce the tidings of joy, since she was the root of joy and had rightly heard, "Rejoice, you who are full of grace, the Lord is with you." For it was not right that what had been so wisely arranged and commanded should go unfulfilled, even if those who heard did not believe. This disbelief often follows when the miracles reported are extraordinary. For they would not have stayed idle if they had believed. But the Magdalene, going along with the Theotokos and hurrying likewise to make the report, experienced something human. Peter was arrested by Herod, freed from his chains by the angel without any effort of his own, got outside the prison and walked a long way, even passing through the city gate, and still did not think that what was happening was real, but thought he was seeing a vision. In the same way she too reckoned the extraordinary miracle as something, as it were, [?]. At the same time the guards had arrived first and begun to weave, with the chief priests, their slander against the resurrection. She surely caught something of this being whispered about and let thoughts of doubt in. Neglecting the report and the Saviour's command, she went to the tomb early, while it was still dark, as John says. The Lord allowed Thomas to say in his unbelief, "Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe." Through Thomas's inquisitive unbelief and his touching, we were confirmed in faith: we believe that Emmanuel was raised in the very body in which he suffered, and we dismiss the Docetists' fables that his body was only an appearance. In the same way the Lord allowed Mary Magdalene, who had slipped back into unbelief and very easily suffered this (for the slipperiness of women's nature is well known), to make the miracle of the resurrection more credible through her curious searching, though it is a miracle beyond faith and all reasoning. After this she came with a doubting mind, and saw only the stone rolled away

from the door of the tomb, and no angel sitting on it as before. So she let unbelief prevail, thinking the sight and her trance had been an illusion, false and not real. She ran to Peter and to the other disciple, whom Jesus loved, and cried out, "They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and I do not know where they have laid him." You see how, having heard something of this kind noised about from the stories the Jews made up by night after the guards' report, her reasoning was led astray. She thought that the adversaries had stolen the body of Jesus in order to pin the theft on the apostles. But Peter and John readily got up and ran to the tomb. What she said was not incredible, as the resurrection was, so that they would disbelieve it. On the contrary, it was believable and quite in keeping with Jewish villainy. They did this fearlessly, since it was quiet and still dark, and they had taken courage from God. But when they came they found clear signs of the resurrection. They saw the linen cloths lying in the tomb, and this would never have happened if the body had been stolen. First, thieves like to strip the dead. Second, they like to carry out the theft very quickly, so as not to be caught and suffer the most terrible penalties. John has written roughly this about the body of Jesus: "They bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews." How could it not have been hard work for thieves to undo the bindings and strip the linen cloths off the body? They were stuck to it and hard to pull away, and would have torn before they came off, for they had been bound together with the mixture of aloes and myrrh that Nicodemus brought. Moreover, the napkin that had been on his head was lying not with the linen cloths but rolled up separately in a place by itself. This showed none of the disturbance there would be if thieves had taken the body. Where would thieves have had such leisure and freedom as to roll up even the head covering neatly and lay it apart? So this too clearly establishes the truth of the resurrection. At the same time it revealed a mystery worthy of God. The head stands for the Godhead, according to the saying, "The head of Christ is God." The doctrines concerning the Godhead remain, even after the Incarnation, as it were wrapped up and undissolved, even though the lower things, which concern the dispensation in the flesh and his life on earth among men (of which the linen cloths were a type), have been unwrapped and handled as far as is possible for us. When Peter and his companion saw these things they believed, and not simply believed: they beheld them with a higher, apostolic mind. For the tomb was full of light, so that although it was still night they saw what was inside in two ways, with the senses and with the spirit. For if, as it is written, there is light for the righteous continually, much more is there light

for the God of the righteous. "But they did not believe," he says, "for as yet they did not know the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead." And yet they did know, since the Saviour had often told them beforehand that he would rise. But they were not persuaded by the Scripture and the oracles found there, which could not fail to be fulfilled; they were still faltering in faith. That Jesus rose naked, without the linen cloths, shows that he would no longer be known according to the flesh as one needing food or drink or the covering of clothes. He had willingly subjected himself to these things in fulfilling the dispensation, since he shared the same nature as us. It also shows the restoration of Adam to his original state, when he was naked in paradise and was not ashamed. For from then on, as God, though incarnate, he was clothed in glory most befitting God, being himself the one who "covers himself with light as with a garment," as the prophet David says. Peter and John, assured by what they had seen, went back home, but they said nothing to Mary. For the only wise one was arranging that, since she disbelieved, she would be won over by sight rather than by hearing. So she stood outside by the tomb weeping. Stooping down, she saw two angels in white, shining garments, sitting one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain. Though she ought to have turned her lament into gladness, she did not stop weeping, so that the angels said, as if in rebuke, "Woman, why are you weeping?" It was as if they were saying, "These tears are womanish, not the tears of a sensible mind. What room is there for lamenting after such a sight?" She was still held by the same unbelief, for the affliction was prolonged so that, by things shown to her little by little, she might be fully purified for faith. She said to them, "They have taken my Lord out of the tomb, and I do not know where they have laid him." When she had said this she turned around and saw Jesus standing there, and did not know that it was Jesus. Partly her sight was darkened by tears and weighed down as if by a mist, and partly Jesus was arranging that she should not recognize him. So he said, "Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you looking for?" Supposing he was the gardener, she said to him, "Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away." Perhaps it was not unfitting that she supposed Jesus was the gardener. For in truth he himself was the true and immortal husbandman of paradise. In the garden of the tomb, as in paradise, he was setting right the woman who through unbelief had deceived Adam, the first gardener. So all these things are full of mystery and of diviner, lofty meanings.

But when Mary had said this, and was distraught over the search for the body, and had turned away instead so as to leave, he saw her tormented [?]. He who pierces to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and who discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart, cut off her unbelief with a single word and sharpened the woman's sight to recognize him. Reproachfully, as he alone knew how, he said only, "Mariam." At once she turned and addressed him, "Rabbouni," which means Teacher, and tried to take hold of those divine feet. And she heard: "Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father." He means: "You had already received the gift of this greeting. You had touched me together with the other Mary, worshipped me and held my feet. Yet you made light of it, so far as even to disbelieve. You thought nothing great of me, and were still looking at the tomb for the one who is from above, divinely with the Father. So now do not touch me, if you still think, with the same mind, that ascending to the Father is something I lack. For in your view I have not yet ascended to my Father. But go to my brothers and tell them, 'I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.'" He means: "Since I have become, according to the flesh, the firstborn among many brothers, I shall ascend bodily to my Father and your Father, my God and your God, not for my own sake now but for yours, my brothers. For if he had not been called my God, seeing in me, as in the firstfruits of the race, the blamelessness of human nature, because I know no sin, he would not have been called your Father, or the God of those who had been estranged from him." That is why Paul too, writing to the Hebrews, said, "For Christ did not enter holy places made with hands, copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us." So Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had said these things to her. After arriving and making her report, she again found Mary the mother of James, and Joanna, and other women with them, hurrying to the tomb with the spices and ointments they had prepared [?]. The darkness had withdrawn and it was deep dawn [?], that is, exactly, just as dawn was first beginning, as Luke says. She joined them and went along. Because of her burning longing for Jesus she seemed to lead them, and she is counted first by the evangelists [?] because of [?]. For she wanted them too to be assured of the resurrection, not from what they had heard from her and the other Mary, but from the divine [?] itself, or from a visitation of angels. So she went with them, wisely keeping silent and saying nothing as they walked along, waiting for the [?] of events, and trusting that they too would be given some personal assurance with their own eyes. When they saw the stone rolled away

from the tomb, they went inside. They did not find the body of Jesus, and while they were perplexed they saw two men in dazzling garments standing by them, and heard from them, "Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen," and the rest. "And returning from the tomb," he says, "they told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest." But since they were a crowd, they disbelieved all the more, and mocked and spurned the report. "For their words seemed to them like idle talk, and they did not believe them." So Peter, roused by their unbelief, and himself somewhat troubled and shaken, ran to the tomb again, stooped down, and once more saw the linen cloths lying there. He had already gone in and looked at them more closely, so he was content just to stoop down. Seeing nothing different, he went away wondering and amazed at what had happened, and glorifying the one who had arranged these things. Then Mary Magdalene went again. At deep dawn she had gone along with the women around Joanna [?], who were carrying the ointments and spices they had prepared before the Sabbath. In the same way she now eagerly ran along, with the same purpose, with Salome, a woman not among the others already named. Salome had bought spices late, but still after the Sabbath, and Mary took Mary the mother of James along with her too, so that she also seemed to have shared in buying the spices. For since they shared the journey, they counted the whole undertaking as shared. "And still very early on the first day of the week they come to the tomb." The word "still" appears in the more accurate copies, showing that this arrival of women at the tomb also took place in addition to those already made. Mark, to clarify "very early," added "when the sun had risen." "And they were saying to one another," he says, "'Who will roll away the stone for us from the door of the tomb?' And looking up they see that the stone has been rolled away, for it was very large." Salome was rightly perplexed, since she had never visited the tomb at all, and she said this to the women walking with her. They kept silent, in the way described above, and lifting their eyes they gave their answer with a look, for the stone could be seen rolled away. Because they made one journey together, it is written that they were perplexed and talked with one another. But we attend to the truth of the history and the nature of the events, and we discern whose particular part it was to be perplexed. For it is implausible that women who had already seen the stone rolled away many times would worry about this. But since, among these women in Mark, Salome appears as the one who did not know, the account is beyond dispute and plausible. For it would not have been consistent for those others either to say, "Who will roll away

…the stone for us," when the Jews had sealed the entrance of the tomb and posted the guard of soldiers, and the third day had come. For those wicked men had said to Pilate: "We remember that that deceiver said while he was still alive, 'After three days I will rise.'" Now if the women knew of the miracle the angel had worked, that the stone had been moved away and the guards had fled, half dead with fear, how could they be at a loss over who would roll the stone away? And if they did not know of the miracle, they should have thought of the military guard, and not pictured the tomb as open. But, as I said, Salome did not know this either, and the words were hers alone. For Mary Magdalene and the other Mary had sat opposite the tomb, as Matthew records, and kept watch there in their loving toil, and had seen with their own eyes both the seals of the Jews and the guard of armed men. Salome went in with the two Marys, and they saw a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe, and all of them were alarmed: Salome because she lacked faith and was disposed in a more human way, the others because they had been coming to the tomb so often and now seemed to be prying into the resurrection more than was fitting. That is why a young man appeared, one whose stature could astonish them and fill them with fear, though by the whiteness of his robe he mingled brightness with the fearsome, as at a festival. And so that they would not be frozen with dread, he spoke to them rather forcefully, teaching them by his words not to be curious after such sights, but rather to stand firm on what they had seen. For he says: "Go, tell his disciples and Peter" (the disciples, because they had often disbelieved; Peter, because he had come to the tomb a second time with the same curiosity as you) "that he is going ahead of you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you." "You" means the women, to whom he had appeared "late on the Sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning," as Matthew wrote. For he is nowhere shown telling the disciples that after his rising he would appear to them in Galilee, unless someone points to what Matthew and Mark wrote. After the mystical supper, when they had sung the hymn and gone out to the Mount of Olives, the Saviour said something like this: "But after I am raised, I will go ahead of you into Galilee." The Marys and Salome came out of the tomb gripped by trembling and astonishment and fled, and they said nothing to anyone. For they were afraid, partly because the young man was so fearsome, and partly because the day was already well advanced and the Jews, as one might expect, were roaming up and down thirsting for blood. In the more accurate copies the Gospel according to Mark
