ends at "For they were afraid." But in some copies this is also added: "Having risen early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons." This seems to contradict what we said earlier. For since the hour of the night at which the Saviour rose is unknown, how can it be written here that he rose "early"? But the passage will not seem contradictory if we read it with understanding. We must punctuate it sensibly, "Having risen," and then go on: "early on the first day he appeared first to Mary Magdalene." Then "having risen" refers to the earlier time, in agreement with Matthew, while "early" belongs to the appearance to Mary, who first saw the Lord with the other Mary and then again alone. For "early" covers the whole stretch of time after cockcrow. There were four times, then, and as many visits, at which the women came to the tomb, and the Holy Spirit arranged that each evangelist should write about one of them. Matthew told of the women who came to the tomb late on the Sabbath, and of the one angel who came down from heaven and rolled away the stone. John wrote that Mary Magdalene came alone in the darkness before dawn and saw two angels inside the tomb. Luke wrote of other women at that same early dawn, and Mark of yet another group as the sun was rising, with some of those who had already come mingled among them. Some saw two men standing beside them, others a young man sitting on the right, but all were clothed in white robes. So someone could put together what each wrote in the order of the times and make one harmony and one body of the whole narrative, as if one person had written it all and not many. If the four had recorded a single visit of the women at a single time and had not said that the same angels appeared, or if all of them had described one and the same appearance, that is, one vision, and said that it happened at different times, each recording a different time, then the account could be accused of disagreement. But the times are different, and so are the persons, and the forms of those who appeared are not the same (for God willed to confirm the incredible miracle of the resurrection in many ways), and what one evangelist did not say another recorded. How then is the whole narrative not pure and free of anything that could be used against it? And since many Marys are mentioned in the Gospels, we should know that there are three in all,

whom John listed together when he said: "Standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene." For we believe that Mary the mother of James and Joses, as the other evangelists call her, is the Theotokos and no one else. The divine birth had to be veiled and kept hidden from the murderous Jews for the sake of the divine plan. That is why the Virgin is recorded to have conceived by the Holy Spirit just as she was about to be led to the bridal chamber, so that Joseph was called her husband and the father of Jesus. In the same way, since Joses and James were sons of Joseph the carpenter by an earlier marriage to a wife who had died, and they were still children, the Theotokos was called and named their mother. This is why the Jews said in their blasphemy against the Saviour: "Is this not the carpenter's son? Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James and Joses and Simon and Judas?" For this reason John, who speaks of God with boldness, called her, as she stood by the cross, the mother of Jesus, as she truly was. The other evangelists were largely concerned with the divine plan, so in keeping with it they called her the mother of James and Joses (for these were the eldest and best known of Joseph's sons). The account clearly shows that because of this arrangement, and the belief that arose from it, Mary could be present at the saving passion without danger. For if most people had known her to be a virgin, she would have been killed by the envious Jews. In the evangelists one can also find her named after just one of Joseph's sons, as "Mary of James" and "Mary of Joses." Mark called her the mother of James the Less and Joses, since there was another James, the son of Alphaeus, who was called "the Great" because he was counted among the twelve apostles. The lesser James was not counted among them. Someone might reasonably raise a further difficulty here. The Saviour promised the disciples, both through the angels and with his own voice, that he would be seen when he came to Galilee. How is it, then, that he appeared and fulfilled the promise in Jerusalem as well? According to Luke, he appeared to the eleven gathered together on the very day of the resurrection. According to John, he appeared both on that day and on the eighth day, standing in their midst and saying, "Peace to you," and letting Thomas touch him. But this shows the richness of his loving generosity. It does not lay him open to a charge of falsehood. For he did not say, "They will see me only in Galilee." Nor did he appear in Jerusalem and then fail to be seen in Galilee as he had promised, for that would have been to break his own word. But if he appeared in Jerusalem as well, to those shut up in a room

for fear of the Jews, who needed his presence, and also fulfilled the promise by appearing in Galilee, then there is no ground for any accusation, since both things were done lovingly and truthfully at once. To me the words in Matthew about the disciples seem to carry great emphasis: "That they should go away into Galilee, and there they will see me." For although he was to appear to them many times, this promise looks to one appearance as special above the others: the one in which he was to appear to them on the mountain. For then, when they had come to him and worshipped him, though some doubted, he said with an authority befitting God: "All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth." What he had by nature as God, he is said to receive as man, in keeping with the divine plan. That is why he also said: "Glorify me, Father, in your presence with the glory which I had with you before the world existed." If he did not have that glory as his own, as God, he could not have received it as someone else's, since God the Father says through the prophet, "My glory I will not give to another." Then he adds the words by which they were to draw the whole world into their net, words that contain the whole mystery of godliness. "Go," he says, "make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to keep all that I have commanded you." And then he adds words that guarantee the fulfilment and outcome of these: "And behold, I am with you always, until the end of the age. Amen." This is why he said: "Tell my brothers to go away into Galilee, and there they will see me." He was pointing, as I said, to this sight as something special and set apart, which he had also announced to them beforehand in other words that are not recorded in the Gospel writings. Otherwise Matthew would not have said: "The eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain to which Jesus had directed them." Yet nowhere in the Gospels does the Lord promise to appear on the mountain. And before this sight on the mountain he also appeared to them by the Sea of Tiberias, which is in Galilee, when there were seven of them: Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee, and two other disciples, as John wrote. But the words "there they will see me" looked to the mountain "to which Jesus had directed them," that is, to the moment when he gave the command befitting God: "Go, make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." Nor does it seem to me beside the point that these words were spoken on a mountain in Galilee and not somewhere else. For in the Greek language "Galilee" means "rolling," and that is why a wheel is called a "gelgel." So, as if from a high mountain,

these words came forth from the Saviour's mouth and rolled like a wheel across the world and ran over the whole of it, and all were baptized, nations and cities, "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." But when the disciples heard these words, they did not go to any nation at once. Instead they stayed in Jerusalem until Pentecost, waiting for the coming of the Holy Spirit, who came upon them in tongues of fire. For Luke says at the beginning of the book of Acts that he appeared to them in various ways over forty days and stayed with them, and "he commanded and charged them not to leave Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, 'which you heard from me; for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.'" The words "not to leave" are very well chosen. They mean not to go far away or to be at a distance. He did not say that they should never go out of Jerusalem at all. How could he have said that, when he had ordered them to go to Galilee? What is said at the end of Luke's Gospel, "And while he was blessing them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven," and likewise what is written in Mark, "So then the Lord, after speaking to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God," must be understood to have happened on the fortieth day, as recorded in Acts. For what the evangelists told in brief in the Gospels is unfolded and made clear in the fuller narrative. These are the matters contained in the Gospel readings of the night of the Lord's Day, which could trouble someone who does not understand them, and so we have laid them before you as a debt we owed. But what you ought to do once you have heard them, I blush to say, when I think of how the crowds rush to the shows and of their frenzy. May the Lord give us strength to turn away from evil and do good, by the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord and God and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

On Holy Easter, and on the Resurrection, delivered on the Great Lord's Day.

Poor people who love festivals welcome celebrations with eager hearts and a proud bearing. Even if they cannot afford the splendour they strive for, they gather every kind of finery from their relatives and acquaintances, and so make sure they lack nothing for the occasion. I think this is what is happening to me today. For I have nothing magnificent of my own to offer to the praises before us,

so I will take refuge in the sacred song we have just sung. I will take my starting points from it and pay my debt, weaving into the words of Scripture my own contributions as well, if this poor servant has any praises of thanksgiving to offer the Master. David has just said, and we with him: "Praise the Lord, all nations; extol him, all peoples." He calls every human being descended from Adam to the hymn and leaves no one outside the call. Westerners, easterners, those on either side, whoever lives near the north or dwells in the south: he gathers them all together with the psalm. Elsewhere he addresses some part of humankind, either calling the holy ones or rousing the children to sing, but here he gathers nations and peoples with the psaltery. For when, as the Apostle says, the form of this world has passed away, and Christ has appeared to all as King and God, when he has fully convinced every unbelieving soul, bridled the tongue of the [?], and put a stop to the folly of the Greeks, the error of the Jews, and the untamable chatter of the heresies, then indeed, then all the nations and the peoples from the beginning of time will bow down and send up an [?] worship. There will be a wonderful harmony of praise, the holy ones singing as they always have, the ungodly pleading because they must. Then truly the hymn of victory will be sung in harmony by all, the conquered and the conquerors alike. Then too the one who caused all the turmoil, who imagined himself to have the Master's rank, will be seen by all as a slave fit for the whip, dragged off to punishment by angels, and all the servants and accomplices of his wickedness will be subjected to fitting punishments and penalties. One alone will appear as King and Judge, acknowledged by all as the common Master. And there will be a hushed stillness, as when a ruler takes his seat on the tribunal, the herald signals for silence, and the people strain their eyes and ears as they wait to hear him speak. Therefore: "Praise the Lord, all nations; extol him, all peoples." Praise him for his power, extol him for his love for humankind. For when we had fallen and were dead, he gave us life again. He renewed the vessel that had suffered, and in his love he refashioned the loathsome remains in the tombs into an incorruptible living being. He brought the soul that had left the body four thousand years before back into its own house, as if from a long journey abroad. Time and forgetfulness have not made it a stranger to its own instrument; it goes back to it faster than a bird flies down to its own nest. Let us speak of what belongs to the feast, so that we may celebrate in a way that is consistent

and fitting to what we celebrate. For what is out of place and foreign is not only useless but disorderly and absurd, and that holds not only in discourses on religion and piety but also in matters outside them and in the wisdom of the world. What orator would be so foolish or so utterly ridiculous that, invited to the gaiety of a wedding, he would abandon fitting and elegant speeches that share in the joy of the festivities, and instead sing mournful laments and bewail the bridal chamber with the woes of tragedy? Or, on the other hand, if he were appointed to perform the customary rites for someone who had died, would forget the grief and turn cheerful before a gathering full of sorrow? If order and skill are good in worldly affairs, surely they are much more fitting in great and heavenly things. Christ, then, rose today: God, the impassible, the immortal. (Wait a little, pagan, and hold back your rash laughter until you have heard everything.) He did not suffer under compulsion, nor was he forced to come down from heaven, nor did he find the resurrection beyond his hopes, as an unexpected favour. He knew the end of all things and began accordingly. Before the eyes of his Godhead he held knowledge of what lay ahead, and even before he came down from heaven he saw the turmoil of the nations, the hardness of Israel, Pilate presiding on the tribunal, Caiaphas tearing his robes at him, the rebellious mob inflamed, Judas betraying him, Peter fighting in his defence, and himself, a little later, transformed by the resurrection into the glory of incorruption. Though all that was to come was sketched out in his knowledge, he did not postpone his grace toward humanity or put off the divine plan. Think of people who see a weak man being swept along by a torrent. They know that one may be caught in the mud of the stream and take blows from the stones the water drives along, yet out of compassion for the man in danger they do not hesitate to go in. In the same way our loving Saviour willingly accepted insults and dishonour in order to save the one who was perishing through deceit. He came down into this life because he knew beforehand that his ascent would also be glorious. He allowed himself to die in his humanity because he also foreknew his rising. For he did not, like an ordinary man, take a reckless risk and leave the outcome to the uncertainty of the future. As God, he arranged what lay before him on fixed and known terms. "This, then, is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it," not with drunkenness and revelry, not with dancing and drunken excess, but with godlike thoughts. Today one can see the whole world as one household, in the harmony of one

…shaken out of its customary business, and turned at a single signal to eager prayer. The highways have no travellers; today the sea is empty of sailors and voyagers. The farmer has thrown down his spade and his plough and dressed himself in festal clothes. The shops are closed for trade. Our troubles have melted away, as winter does when spring appears, and the noise, turmoil and storms of life have given way to the peace of the feast. The poor man dresses up like the rich; the rich man appears more splendid than usual; the old man runs like a youth to share in the gladness; the sick man pushes past his illness. The child keeps the feast with his senses by changing his clothes, since he cannot yet keep it with his mind. The virgin's soul is overjoyed, because she sees the remembrance of her own hope honoured so brilliantly. The married woman rejoices as she keeps the feast with her whole household, for now she, her husband, the children, the servants and everyone in the house are glad. A young swarm of bees, newly hatched, flies out of the hiding place of the hives into the air and the light for the first time and clusters all together on a single branch of a tree. In the same way, at this feast whole families run together to their homes. Truly the present day is a fitting image of the day to come, for both gather people together: that one gathers all people universally, this one gathers them in their separate groups. In fact, to speak more truly, in brightness and good cheer this day is more gracious than the one we await. On that day the mourners must be seen too, those whose sins are uncovered, but today's delight admits nothing gloomy. The righteous man rejoices, and the man whose conscience is not clean waits to be set right through repentance. All grief is put to sleep on this day, and no one is so sorrowful that he finds no relief in the magnificence of the feast. Now the prisoner is released, the debtor is forgiven, and the slave is set free by the good and kindly proclamation of the Church. He is not shamefully slapped on the cheek and released from blows by a blow. He is not displayed to the people on a high platform as if in a procession, so that his freedom begins with insult and blushing. Instead he is released with such decorum that [?] even the one who still remains in slavery is benefited. His sins may be many and grievous, beyond excuse and pardon, but the master reveres the calm and kindness of the day and takes back the one who was cast off and counted among the disgraced, as Pharaoh took back the cupbearer from the prison. For he knows that at the appointed time of the resurrection, whose likeness we honour in this day, he too will need the forbearance and goodness of the Master. By lending mercy here, he expects to be repaid in due season. You have heard, you masters: keep this word, for it is good. Do not slander me to your slaves as one who praises the day falsely. Take away the

grief of afflicted souls, as the Lord took away the deadness of bodies. Change the dishonoured into honour, the afflicted into joy, and those who dare not speak into boldness. Bring out of the corner those who have been cast aside, as [?]. Let the beauty of the feast bloom like a flower for everyone. If the birthday of a human king opens the prison, will the day of victory of the risen Christ not release the afflicted? You poor, welcome the one who feeds you. You whose bodies are wasted and maimed, welcome the one who heals your misfortunes. It is the hope of the resurrection that makes us pursue virtue and hate vice. If the resurrection were taken away, one saying would prevail everywhere: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” With his eyes on this day the Apostle despises this passing life and longs for the life to come. Belittling the things we see, he says: “If we have hoped in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied.” Because of this day human beings are heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ. Because of this day, whatever part of a body flesh-eating birds devoured a thousand years ago will be found not to be missing. Whatever whales and dogs and sea creatures fed on will rise again together with the man when he is raised. So will whatever fire burned up and the worm consumed in the tombs. In short, every body that corruption has destroyed since its creation will be given back by the earth complete and intact. And as Paul teaches, the resurrection will be accomplished in the twinkling of an eye. The twinkling of an eye is the closing of the eyelids, and nothing could be swifter than that. So do not reckon in human terms, by your own power, all the stretches of time you trace in your mind. First, you think, the decayed bones that have turned to earth must be compacted again into hardness and smoothness, joined again from their crumbled state into an ordered harmony, and brought back into their natural connection. Then you picture the flesh wrapped around them, the sinews stretched out to bind them, and the fine channels of veins and arteries spread out beneath the skin. You picture an unspeakable, countless multitude of souls coming from certain secret dwellings, each recognising its own body like a garment set apart for it, quickly taking up residence in it again, and telling it apart without error among such a multitude of kindred spirits. Think of all the souls since Adam, and all the bodies descended from him: a multitude of so many dissolved houses, and of householders returning from a long journey abroad. Yet all of it is accomplished marvellously. The house is not slow to be rebuilt, and the inhabitant does not wander about and camp out of doors, searching

for where his own belongings are. He goes straight to it, like a dove to its own dovecote, even if there are many crowded together in the same place, gleaming with similar shapes. And how do the memory and recollection of the former life, and the awareness of each deed, come back so quickly to a living being that was dissolved so many ages before? After all, even a man woken from a deep sleep does not know for a little while who he is or where he is, and he forgets familiar things, until wakefulness scatters the drowsiness and rekindles his memory and his powers. These thoughts, and others like them, steal into the reasonings of many people and fill the mind with overwhelming wonder, but along with the wonder they bring in unbelief. The mind does not find the solution to what puzzles it and what it is looking for, and it cannot bring its curiosity to rest by finding an answer and settling the matter. So in the weakness of its own reasonings it goes on to unbelief, casting out and rejecting the truth of the facts. Our discourse, proceeding on its way, has now arrived at this much-discussed question, which is proper and closely related to the subject of the present feast. So come, let us take the matter back a little to a fitting starting point, and try to give assurance to those who wrongly doubt what is evident. When the Creator of all things willed to make man, he did not bring him into being as a contemptible creature but as more honourable than all, and he appointed him king of the creation under heaven. Having chosen this, having fashioned him so wise and godlike, and having adorned him with abundant grace, did he really bring him into being with the intention that once born he should be corrupted and undergo complete destruction? Such an aim would be vain, and it is utterly unworthy to attribute such a thought to God. It would make him like children, who build eagerly and quickly pull down what they have made, because their thinking ends in no useful purpose. We have been taught quite the opposite: he created the first-formed man immortal. When transgression and sin came about, he deprived him of immortality as the penalty for the offence. But then the fountain of goodness, overflowing with love for humanity and moved with compassion for the work of his own hands, ordered things [?] with wisdom and knowledge, and was pleased to renew us to our original state. These things are true and worthy of our conception of God, for they bear witness to his power as well as his goodness. To be unfeeling and harsh toward those one rules and shepherds is not fitting even for good and excellent men. So the shepherd wants his flock to be healthy, and

almost immortal. The cowherd raises his cattle with every kind of care, and the goatherd prays that his goats will bear twins. In short, every herdsman longs for his herd to survive and thrive, because he has some useful end in view. This being so, what we have just said has shown that it is entirely fitting for the Creator and Craftsman of our race to refashion the work that was corrupted. It is evident, then, that those who refuse to believe what follows fight against it for one reason only: they think it impossible for God to raise what has died and been dissolved. This is truly the mindset of the dead and senseless. They reckon things impossible and beyond reach for God, and they attribute their own weakness to his almighty majesty. To strike at their folly with arguments that refute it, let us prove the future, disbelieved event from things that have happened and exist. You have heard that dust was moulded and became a man. Then teach me, I beg you, you who claim to grasp everything with your own wisdom: how was the fine, scattered dust gathered together? How did earth become flesh, and how did the same matter make bones and skin and fat and hair? Though the flesh is one, how are the members different in form, in qualities and in texture? How is the lung soft to the touch and livid in colour, the liver dense and red, and the heart compact and the hardest part of the flesh? How is the spleen loose and black, and the omentum white and woven together like a fishing net by [?]? Let us also consider this: how did the first woman come into being as a complete living creature from a small piece of the rib, like the perfect [?] first one? The part was enough for everything, and the little made up the whole. The rib became head, hands and feet, the winding and intricate structure of the entrails, flesh and hair, eye and nose and mouth. In short, so as not to draw the discourse out too long, everything there is marvellous and astonishing to us, who are of little power, but for God the principles of its construction lie ready to hand and are entirely clear. How then can anyone think them sensible, who grant that a single rib became a human being but refuse to believe that the same human being is re-created from the whole of his own matter? It is not possible, it is not possible, to pry into God's workings with human notions. If everything were comprehensible to us, the one who is greater than us would not be greater. But why speak of God? We cannot even compare with the irrational animals in certain powers, but fall short of them too. Horses and dogs and many others outrun us; camels and mules surpass us in strength, and donkeys in remembering roads; and the sharp sight of the gazelle is not found in our eyes.

So it is the part of grateful and sensible people to believe what God says, and not to demand the manner and causes of his workings, since these are beyond us. One of these busybodies will be told: “Show me by your reasoning how the things we see came into being. Tell me by what art he fashioned this work of so many forms. If you can discover that, then you have reason to be at a loss and vexed at not understanding the reordering of the regeneration, since you know the principle of the creation. But if those things are a dream and a fantasy to you, and knowledge of them is blocked on every side, do not be indignant that you also fail to grasp how what was corrupted is restored, since you do not know the principle of its construction.” The same Craftsman made the first creation and makes the second reordering. He knows how to fit his own work back together into its original state after it has undergone dissolution. If wisdom is needed, the fountain of wisdom is with him; if power is needed, he requires no co-worker or helper. He is the one who, in the words of the most wise Prophet, measured the water in his hand, the great and immense heaven with a span, and the earth with a handful. Consider these images. They give signs of the working of his ineffable power, and they make our reasonings despair of ever imagining anything worthy of God's nature. He is almighty, and so he is called. Surely you will not quarrel with this, but will grant it as an accepted point. For one who can do all things, nothing is impossible or beyond reach. You have many pledges of faith that compel you to agree with what we say. First, the whole varied and intricate creation cries out more clearly [?] than any proclamation that there is a great and wise Craftsman, who devised everything we see. Besides this, God is provident, and he foresaw from afar the petty souls of unbelievers. So he confirmed the raising of the dead by deeds, bringing many bodies of the dead back to life. That is why Lazarus, four days dead, leapt out of the tomb. That is why the widow's only son was given back to his mother, returned to the living from the bier and the funeral procession. And there were countless others whom it would be tedious to list now. And why speak of our God and Saviour himself, when he even granted his servants the apostles the power to raise the dead, so that the doubters might be put to shame all the more? The proof, then, is plain. So why, you contentious people, do you trouble us as if we were expounding unproven doctrines? As one was raised, so can ten be; as ten, so three hundred; as three hundred, so a multitude. The maker of one statue will easily be the craftsman of ten thousand. Have you not seen how engineers model the shapes and plans of great and extraordinary buildings in a little wax? The principle in the small model has the same power in the many great constructions. The heaven is great, an artful work of God. But since God made man a rational creature,

so that by understanding his works he might glorify their wise and ingenious Maker, you will see the astronomer's globe. It is small, but it turns in the expert's hand just as the heaven is turned by God. The tiniest construction becomes an image of the great creation, and in small things the principle explains what is lofty and beyond our senses. Why have I gone through all this? So that you may know that if you ask me how the bodies of all the ages will rise, you will quickly hear in reply: “How was Lazarus raised after four days?” Clearly a sensible man who accepts the assurance in the one case will accept it equally in the many. Once you grant that God is the one who acts, call nothing impossible, and do not think that the wisdom of the incomprehensible one can be comprehended by your own mind. For nothing is beyond bounds for him, but for you the things of the infinite are unsearchable.

We shall see this argument clearly if, in addition to what has been said, we also examine the way we come into being. I do not mean that first and most ancient creation by God, which we discussed earlier, but the generation that nature has carried out in due order down to the present. This too is baffling and beyond the reach of human reasoning. The seed is a moist substance without form or shape. How does it solidify into a head and harden into shins and ribs? How does it make the soft, porous brain, the bone enclosing it so hard and unyielding, and the whole varied structure of the living creature? I put it briefly, so as not to drag things out by going through every detail. The seed is formless at the beginning, yet it is shaped into a figure and grows [?] into bulk, fashioned by the ineffable art of God. In the same way it is not at all unlikely, but entirely consistent, that the matter in the tombs, which once had form, should be renewed again into its old shape, and that the dust should once more become a man, just as it had its origin from dust in the first place. Let us grant God as much power as a potter has. Consider what the potter does. He takes shapeless clay and works it into a vessel, then sets it out in the sun's rays to dry it and make it solid. The thing he has moulded may be a small jar, a dish or a storage jar. But if someone stumbles into it and knocks it over, it falls and breaks and becomes shapeless. Yet if the craftsman wishes, he quickly repairs the accident. He shapes the clay again by his art and produces a vessel no worse than the one that existed before. This potter is a small creature of God's power, yet God is not believed when he

promises to renew the dead. This is great folly. Let us also consider the example of the wheat, by which Paul, the all-wise, teaches the foolish when he says: “Fool! What you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of some other kind of seed; but God gives it a body as he has willed.” Let us pay careful attention to how wheat comes into being, and perhaps we shall learn the principle of the resurrection. The grain of wheat is thrown into the earth. It rots in the moisture and, as one might say, dies, and ends up as a milky substance. When this thickens a little it becomes a sharp white point, and when it has grown enough to peep out of the earth, it changes from white to a gentle green. Then it becomes grass, the hair of the clods. Spreading over them and branching out moderately, it nourishes a many-branched root below, preparing a foundation in advance for the weight to come. The masts of ships are braced on every side by many ropes, so that they stay firm, held by pulls that balance each other. In the same way the rope-like shoots of the root become supports and props for the ears. When the wheat has risen into a stalk and is pressing upward, God props it up with joints and knots, as one secures a house with tie-beams, because of the weight the head is expected to carry. Then, when its strength is ready, he splits the sheath and brings forth the ear. And there again are greater wonders. The grains grow around the ear in rows, and each grain has its own storehouse. Last of all the awns are thrust out, sharp and fine. They are weapons, I think, against seed-picking birds, so that the birds will be pricked by their points and not ravage the fruit. Do you see what wonders a single grain works when it rots, and how many it rises with, though it fell alone? A human being, by contrast, takes on nothing more; he only receives back what he had. For this reason our renewal appears easier than the growing of wheat. From here, go on to consider the trees, and how each year winter becomes a kind of death for them. The fruit drops off, the leaves fall, and the wood is left dry, stripped of all its grace. But when springtime arrives, the loveliest blossom springs up on them, and after the blossom comes the covering of leaves. Then, as a beautiful sight, the tree draws people's eyes and becomes a workshop for songbirds, which perch in its foliage, and a wonderful grace shines around it. Many people have even left houses adorned with gold and with Thessalian and Laconian marble, and found it more delightful to spend their time under the trees. That is why the patriarch Abraham pitched his tent under an oak. It was not at all that he lacked a house; he delighted in the pleasure of the branches.

[?] Gregory of Nyssa. The life of reptiles also leads me to agree with the argument before us. In winter the spark of life in them is deadened, and for six months they lie in their dens completely motionless. But when the appointed time comes and thunder resounds through the world, they take the crash as a kind of signal for life, spring up swiftly, and after a long interval go about their usual activities again. What is the reason for this? Let the one who puts God's works to the test and passes judgment on them tell me. Let him teach me how thunder lets snakes be roused when they are dead, and yet does not let human beings be brought to life when God's trumpet sounds from heaven, as the divine word says: "For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised." And elsewhere, more clearly: "And he will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect." So let us not disbelieve in changes and renewals. The life of plants and of various animals, and indeed of human beings themselves, teaches us that nothing subject to decay and coming-to-be stays the same; everything is in a state of alteration and change. First, if you like, let us look at the change we undergo as we grow older. We know what a nursing infant is like. After a little while it gains the power to crawl, and it is no different from little puppies, propped up on four limbs. Around its third year it stands upright and lets out a lisping, stammering voice. Then it forms its words clearly and becomes a charming boy. From that age it passes on to adolescence and youth. Down covers the cheek, and soon a shaggy beard follows, and he becomes one person after another. Then he is a man in his prime, rugged and hardy. But when four decades have passed, the first sign of decline whitens [?] the head, and strength gives way to weakness. Last of all comes old age, the complete extinction of strength. The body bends and stoops toward the ground like ears of grain that have dried out too much, the smooth skin becomes wrinkled, and the man who was once a youth and a champion is an infant again, lisping, witless, crawling on hands and feet as he did long ago. What do you think all this is? Is it not alteration? Are these not changes of many kinds? Are these not novelties of every sort, transforming the mortal creature even before death? And our sleeping and waking: how could they fail to teach the wise about the question before us? For sleep is an image of death, and waking is an imitation of resurrection. That is why some of the wise outside our faith called sleep the brother of death, because what happens to us in each state is so alike. In both alike there is forgetfulness and ignorance of

what is past and what is to come. The body lies without sensation. It does not recognize a friend or know an enemy, and it does not see those who stand around and look at it. It lies limp, dead, without any activity, no different from those laid in tombs and coffins. You may rob the sleeper as though he were dead, if you wish: you may empty his house or put chains on him, and he has no awareness of what is being done. But a little later, when this state lets up and eases off, the man rises as if he had just been brought back to life. Little by little he comes to awareness of himself and of things around him. Slowly he takes up his activities again, as though the kindling of wakefulness were giving him a soul once more. While the creature still exists and survives, so many trances, alterations, changes, [?] and rememberings are bound up with its life, by night and by day. Given this, it is very foolish and quarrelsome not to believe God when he promises the final renewal, since he is the one who made the first creation. What most of all stands in the way of the objectors, and inclines them to disbelieve, is above all, I think, the belief that bodies are utterly annihilated. But this is not so. They are not completely annihilated. They are dissolved into the things they were made of, and they exist in water, air, earth and fire. The primary elements remain, and what came from them returns to them after dissolution, so the parts are preserved in the wholes. Now it is easy enough for God to create out of nothing (that is how all things came into being in the beginning). It is surely far easier and simpler for him to bring things into being from principles that already exist. So let us not destroy humanity's fair hope: the restoration of our weakness, and the second birth, so to speak, that is free from death. Nor let us insult God's good and loving promise through an excessive love of pleasure. Those who oppose the present subject seem to me to be companions of vice and enemies of virtue. They are lustful and greedy, with no restraint over eyes, hearing or smell, and they let pleasure stream in upon them through all their senses. The doctrine of the resurrection carries with it the judgment to come, and they hear the sacred books saying plainly that our life is not free of accountability. When we are renewed to the second life, we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, to receive from him as judge the due reward for how we have lived. These men are conscious of the most shameful deeds, deserving of many punishments, and because they hate the judgment, they abolish the resurrection as well. They are like the wicked servants who squandered their lord's property and imagine for themselves the death and ruin of their master, inventing empty reasonings to suit their own desires.

But no one of sound mind thinks [?] this way. Otherwise, what use is justice, and [?], and kindness, and everything good? Why [?] do people toil and live as philosophers? Why do they bring the pleasures of the belly under control, love self-restraint, take only a little sleep, and battle against winter cold and stifling heat, if there is no resurrection? Shall we answer them with the words of Paul: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die"? If there is no resurrection, and death is the end of life, then away with accusations and reproaches! Give the murderer free licence. Let the adulterer plot against marriages openly. Let the greedy man revel at his rivals' expense. Let no one rebuke the slanderer. Let the perjurer swear false oaths constantly, since death awaits the man who keeps his oath as well. Let someone else lie as much as he likes, since truth bears no fruit. Let no one pity the poor, since mercy goes unrewarded. Such ideas produce a confusion worse than the Flood. They drive out every sober thought and sharpen every mad and murderous intention. If there is no resurrection, there is no judgment either. If judgment is done away with, the fear of God is driven out along with it. And where fear does not keep people sober, there the devil dances with sin. Very fittingly did David write that psalm about such people: "The fool has said in his heart, 'There is no God.' They are corrupt and have become abominable in their practices." If there is no resurrection, then these are all a myth: Lazarus and the rich man, the dreadful chasm, the unquenchable blaze of fire, the burning [tongue?] [?], the longed-for drop of water and the poor man's finger. For it is plain that all these things depict the resurrection to come. The [tongue?] and the finger are not understood as members of the bodiless soul, but as parts of the body. And let no one suppose that these things have already happened. They are a foretelling of what is to come. They will happen at the time when the world's new ordering gives life back to the dead and brings each person to account for how he lived, composite as before, made up of soul and body. And Ezekiel, inspired by God and a witness of great visions: what meaning was he led toward when he saw that great, wide plain full of human bones, over which he was commanded to prophesy? Flesh at once grew around them, and the bones that had been loosed and scattered in disorder were joined to one another in order and harmony. Is it not plain that through such words he shows us clearly enough that this very flesh will return to life? Those who are contentious about this doctrine seem to me not only impious but out of their minds. Words like resurrection, return to life and new ordering all direct the hearer's mind to the body, which is subject to decay. For the soul, considered in itself,

will never rise again, since it does not die. It is incorruptible and indestructible. But though it is immortal, the partner in its deeds is mortal. For this reason, before the just judge at the time of reckoning, it will once more dwell in its fellow worker, so that together with it the soul may receive the shared punishments or honours. Or rather, to make our argument still more consistent, let us look at it this way. What do we mean by a human being: both together, or one of the two? It is plain that the union of the two is what defines this living creature. There is no need to dwell at length on what is undisputed and well known. That being so, let us also consider this. When people commit adultery, murder, theft and everything that goes with them, or on the other hand practise temperance, self-control and every activity opposed to vice, do we say that these deeds are the work of both? Or do we confine them to the soul alone? Here too the truth is plain. Nowhere does the soul split off from the body to practise theft or to break into a house. Nor again does it give bread to the hungry by itself, or give drink to the thirsty, or hurry without hesitation to the prison to care for someone suffering there. In every action, both lay hold of the work together and accomplish together what is done. Since this is so, how can you grant that there will be a judgment on how we have lived, and yet tear the one from the other? When the deeds are shared, how can you confine the trial to the soul alone? If someone were to judge human offences precisely, and carefully examine where the first causes of sin spring from, he would perhaps find that the body is the first offender in the charges. Often, when the soul is at rest and enjoys an untroubled calm, the eye has looked with passion at things it would have been better not to see. It has passed the disease on to the soul and turned its quiet into storm and surging waves. In the same way the ears, when they hear indecent or provoking words, pour the mire of agitation or disorder into the thoughts, as if through pipes. Sometimes the nose too, through its sense and the vapours it takes in, does great and inconceivable harm to the inner man. Hands also know how to weaken the firmness of a steadfast soul by their touch. As I go through it little by little and examine it in this way, I find that the poor body is to blame for many sins. But the body also bears the labours of virtue and toils in the contests for what is good. It is cut with iron, burned with fire, torn with whips and weighed down with grievous chains, and it endures every outrage so as not to betray the sacred philosophy, like a city with fine towers surrounded by the war of vice. If, then, it toils with the soul in good deeds, and

is not left out of its sins, on what grounds do you bring the bodiless soul alone before the court? This argument is neither just nor sensible. If the soul sinned alone and naked, the judge will punish it alone. But if it plainly has an accomplice, the judge, being just, will not let that accomplice go free. I also hear Scripture saying that just punishments will be laid on the condemned: fire, darkness and the worm. All of these are punishments for composite, material bodies. Fire could never touch a soul by itself, nor could darkness distress it, since it has no eyes or organs of sight. And what could a worm do, since it destroys bodies, not spirits? Therefore, by consistent reasoning, we are driven from every side to accept the raising of the dead. God will accomplish it at the appointed times, confirming his own promises by deeds. Let us, then, believe him who says: "For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised." And again: "The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and will come out: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment." He does not only promise. By the works he carries out day by day he also teaches clearly that he is almighty. He did not grow weary when he created in the beginning, and he will not lack wisdom when he transforms. Let us consider what is before us now, and we will not disbelieve what is to come. Every work of God is followed by amazement, and the wonder is great and beyond words when we see the likenesses of fathers and great-grandfathers passing exactly into the features of their descendants, and children becoming copies of their forefathers. Then I am utterly astonished at the all-wise art of God, the supreme craftsman and Saviour. Copies of originals that no longer exist or appear are created and refashioned in an ineffable mystery, and through the working of these patterns they raise up the dead, as it were, in other people. Often the traits of many people together are reproduced in one body: the father's nose, the grandfather's eye, the uncle's walk, the mother's voice. One person then looks like a plant that has taken grafts from many trees and bears countless kinds of fruit for those who gather it. All these things are marvellous, and how they happen is unknown to us. Yet for the Creator they are close at hand, and he accomplishes them, as we know, with great ease. It is therefore very absurd and ignorant to grant that the features of bodies already rotted and decayed rise again in those born every day, and that what belongs to some passes over to others, and yet to refuse to agree that what is one's own and proper will be renewed and restored to life in the very people who once possessed it. It is absurd to deny this and fight against it, and to treat as a myth, not a sound teaching, the promise of the one who established this whole visible world and
ordered it as he willed. But we have believed in the resurrection, and we send up glory to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

On the Holy and Saving Pascha. The true rest of the Sabbath has now reached its end. This is the Sabbath that received God's blessing, on which the Lord rested from his own works, keeping Sabbath in the inactivity of death for the salvation of the world. It has shown its grace to eyes and ears and heart, for the feast was celebrated for us through all of these: through what we saw, through what we heard, and through the gladness we welcomed into our hearts. What the eyes saw was light, carried before us through the night by the torches, as by a pillar of fire. The word that sounded in our ears all night long in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs flowed like a stream of joy through our hearing into the soul, and filled us with good hopes. And the heart, gladdened by what was said and seen, took the imprint of the blessedness that cannot be described, led by the hand through what is visible toward what is invisible. So the good things of this rest are an image of those good things that no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived, and by themselves they give assurance of the unspeakable hope of what is stored up for us. This radiant night has mingled the light of the lamps with the sun's morning rays and made one continuous day, not divided by any interval of darkness. So let us understand, brothers, the prophecy that says: "This is the day which the Lord has made." There is one task, and it is nothing heavy or hard to accomplish. It is joy, gladness and exultation, for so the word says: "Let us exult and be glad in it." What good things! What sweet legislation! Who would put off obeying such commands? Who would not count even a short delay a loss? Gladness is the task and exultation is the command, and by them the condemnation for sin is undone and sorrows are turned into joy. This is the saying of Wisdom: "In the day of gladness evils are forgotten." This day has made us forget the first sentence passed against us. Or rather, it has annihilated it, not merely made us forget it, for it has wiped out every memory of our condemnation completely. Then childbirth came with pains; now birth is without labour. Then we were born of flesh as flesh; now what is born is spirit, from the Spirit. Then we were born sons of men; now we are born children of God. Then we were cast down from heaven to earth;

now the heavenly one has made us heavenly too. Then death reigned through sin; now righteousness takes power in its turn through life. Then one man opened death's entrance; now through one man life is brought in instead. Then through death we fell from life; now death is destroyed by life. Then out of shame we hid beneath the fig tree; now in glory we draw near to the tree of life. Then through disobedience we were banished from paradise; now through faith we come inside paradise. Once more the fruit of life is set before us to enjoy freely. Once more the spring of paradise, divided into four by the rivers of the Gospels, waters the whole face of the Church. It drenches the furrows of our souls, which the sower of the word has cut with the plough of teaching, and it multiplies the harvest of virtue. What, then, should we do in response? What else but imitate the prophetic mountains and hills with our leaping? For "the mountains," it says, "skipped like rams, and the hills like lambs of the flock." So come, let us exult in the Lord. He has destroyed the enemy's power and set up for us the great trophy of the cross over the fallen adversary. Let us raise a shout! A shout is a cry of victory, raised by the victors over the vanquished. The enemy's battle line has fallen. The one who commanded the wicked army of demons has gone and vanished and has now passed into nothingness. So let us say: "The Lord is a great God, and a great king over all the earth." He has blessed the crown of the year with his goodness and gathered us into this spiritual choir, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory for ever.

On the [?] and Holy Resurrection of Our Lord and God. Blessed be God. Let us praise today the only-begotten God, the begetter of the heavenly beings, who peered out from the hidden depths of the earth and covered the whole world with his light-bearing rays. Let us praise today the burial of the Only-begotten, the resurrection of the victor, the joy of the world, the life of the nations of the world. Let us praise today the one who clothed himself in sin. Let us praise today God the Word. He refuted the wisdom of the world, confirmed what the prophets foretold, gathered the band of the apostles together, and spread abroad the calling of the Church and the grace of the Spirit. For look: we who were once strangers to the knowledge of God have come to know God, and what is written has been fulfilled: "All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord" [?]

“And all the families of the nations shall worship before him.” What will they remember? The old fall and the new resurrection; the ancient transgression and the later setting right; the death brought by Eve and the birth from the Virgin; the restoration of the nations, the forgiveness of sinners, the [?] of the [?], the foretelling of the prophets, the preaching of the apostles, the rebirth of the font, the entry into paradise, the return to heaven; the Creator rising again, the one who stripped off the unsightliness, who by God's mighty work changed the perishable into imperishability. And what unsightliness [?]? The one Isaiah spoke of: “And we saw him,” he says, “and he had no form or beauty. But his form was without honor, falling short of the sons of men.” When was he without honor? When he talked with the wicked Jews and was called a Samaritan and one who had a demon; when Judas Iscariot and the offspring of darkness seized the One whom nothing can contain, in order to murder him. Not without reason did John say to them, “Offspring of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?” For truly the wrath of God will remain upon them. When was he without honor? When the shoot of gentleness was struck in the face, and they questioned under oath the one who is the judge of oaths. When was he without honor? When the Judge was put on trial and the Judge of the world was judged; the servant questioned and the Master kept silent; the light was still and the darkness exulted; the creature grew bold and the Creator endured. When was he without honor? When the bulls gored and the calf stood by; when the lion roared and the bulls exulted, as it is written: “Many calves have surrounded me, fat bulls have closed me in. They opened their mouth against me, like a lion ravening and roaring.” When was he without honor? When the dogs barked and the Master bore it; when the wolves snatched and the sheep stood by; when a robber was called to life and the Life of the world was dragged to death; when they shouted that unruly and deadly cry, “Away with him, away with him, crucify him! His blood be on us and on our children!” The Lord-slayers, the prophet-slayers, the fighters against God, the haters of God, the outragers of the law, the enemies of grace, the strangers to the faith of their fathers, the advocates of the devil, the offspring of the

demons, the accursed, the utterly wicked, the [?], the haters of the good! Small wonder that they cried, “Away with him, away with him, crucify him!” For the coming of the Godhead in the flesh galled them, and the manner of his rebukes grieved them; for it is the way of sinners to hate meeting the righteous. When was he without honor? When they scourged him and tortured his holy body, as he bore his suffering willingly, so that he might heal the old wounds of our sins; when the wood of the

cross, the trophy of victory over the devil, he carried on his shoulders; when they put a crown of thorns on the one who crowns those who trust in him; when they clothed in purple the one who grants incorruption to those reborn through water and the Holy Spirit; when they nailed to the wood the one who is Lord of life and death. When was he without honor? When the soldiers made a mock triumph over the Master of the army of heaven. When was he without honor? When they put a sponge on a reed, filled it with vinegar and gave him to drink, and gave gall to the one who had rained manna down upon them; when the rocks were split and the veil of the temple was torn, struck with horror at the daring of the wicked; when the sun mourned and put on darkness like sackcloth, mourning the falling away of the Jews. For the day lamented the calamities of the Jews, when the Life hung between robbers, one of them reviling and slandering, the other stealing paradise by repentance. When was he without honor? When the body was handed over for burial. When was he without honor? When soldiers stood guard and the earth hid the one who had founded the earth upon the waters; when the apostles went into hiding, unable to bear the weight of their trials. But see, beloved, the wonders of God, and after the passion the triumphs of joy. The one without honor was changed into glory, and the joy of the world has been raised imperishable together with the body. Then the earth was in labor, and the day was big with child, and death spat out the life of all. For it was not possible for the one who rules all things by his word to be held fast by death. Let us therefore celebrate the resurrection on the third day, which brings us eternal life. For just as Mary the Mother of God, without loosening the bonds of her virgin, unwedded womb, by the will of God and the grace of the Spirit gave birth to the Maker of the ages, God the Word from God, so also the earth, loosing the pangs of death from its own womb, spat out at the word of command the Master of the Jews; for it could not hold a body that had become a vessel of immortality. So the prophet David, looking ahead to the restoring of majesty, the undoing of death, and the freedom of those who were once slaves, cries out and says, “The Lord has become king; he has clothed himself with majesty.” What majesty did he clothe himself with? Incorruption, immortality, the assembly of the apostles, the crown of the Church. No longer

[?] the earth [?] sin; our Lord Jesus Christ, having risen as he had foretold, made it firm by the wood of the cross, so that it should no longer walk on the slippery path to destruction, nor be tossed by the storms of error. Let us bring forward the blessed Paul as a witness to this, who says plainly, “For this perishable body must put on imperishability.” That is why the Psalmist also says, “Your throne has been prepared from of old; you are from everlasting”; and, “Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, which shall not be destroyed”; and again, “Your kingdom is a kingdom of all the ages”; and again, “The Lord has become king; let the earth rejoice, let the many islands be glad.” For to him belong the glory and the might. Amen.
